questions.question: When does F_p contain a primitive n-th root of unity (so an n-point NTT can exist)?
options: When n divides p-1
When p divides n
When n is prime
When p equals n plus one
questions.explanation: F_p* is cyclic of order p-1. A subgroup (and generator) of order n exists exactly when n divides p-1.

questions.question: What makes an n-th root of unity ω "primitive"?
options: Its multiplicative order is exactly n
It is the smallest residue with ω^n = 1
It satisfies ω^n = 0 in F_p
It is always equal to a primitive root modulo p
questions.explanation: Primitive means ω generates the full cyclic subgroup of size n, so its multiplicative order must be n, not a proper divisor.

questions.question: In an iterative Cooley–Tukey NTT stage of size len, what is the correct per-stage twiddle base wlen?
options: wlen = ω^(n/len) mod p
wlen = ω^(len/n) mod p
wlen = ω^len mod p
wlen = ω^(n*len) mod p
questions.explanation: At stage len, butterflies need powers stepping by n/len so the stage uses the (len)-th principal root derived from the n-th root ω.

questions.question: Which two changes are required to turn a forward NTT into its inverse?
options: Use ω^{-1} instead of ω, then multiply every output by n^{-1}
Reverse the input list, then subtract every butterfly output
Use ω instead of ω^{-1}, then add n to every output
Run the same code twice, then divide by p
questions.explanation: The inverse uses the inverse root of unity and a final scaling by 1/n in the field, because the DFT matrix inverse is (1/n) times the conjugate/inverse-root matrix.

questions.question: Why is it not enough for ω to satisfy ω^n = 1 for an n-point NTT?
options: If ω is not primitive, the transform matrix loses rank and becomes non-invertible
Non-primitive ω makes modular addition undefined
Non-primitive ω forces p to be even
If ω is not primitive, all outputs become zero
questions.explanation: If ω has order dividing n but smaller than n, powers repeat too early. That creates collisions and the NTT cannot be inverted.

questions.question: An implementation uses ω of order n/2 for an n-point transform. What concrete failure should you expect?
options: Two different inputs can produce the same transformed output (a collision)
All inputs map to distinct outputs but the inverse is slower
The transform still inverts correctly but outputs are permuted
Only the last coefficient is wrong because of wrap-around
questions.explanation: Order n/2 means the twiddle factors repeat with period n/2, so the transform cannot distinguish certain input patterns and is not one-to-one.

questions.question: What ring does a standard NTT-based convolution naturally implement?
options: F_p[x]/(x^n - 1) (cyclic convolution)
F_p[x]/(x^n + 1) (negacyclic convolution) without any extra steps
F_p[x]/(x^n) (truncated convolution)
F_p[x]/(Φ_n(x)) for any n, with no parameter constraints
questions.explanation: Using an n-th root of unity diagonalizes cyclic shifts, which corresponds to multiplication modulo x^n - 1.

questions.question: To use an NTT for negacyclic multiplication in F_p[x]/(x^n + 1) with n a power of two, what extra root condition is typically required?
options: A primitive 2n-th root ψ in F_p (so 2n divides p-1)
A primitive n-th root ω in F_p (so n divides p+1)
A prime n so the transform length is prime
A composite modulus p so x^n + 1 factors
questions.explanation: Negacyclic convolution can be reduced to a cyclic NTT by twisting with a primitive 2n-th root ψ where ω = ψ^2. Existence requires 2n | (p-1).
